options: A template constructor deletes the defaulted copy constructor; write the copy by hand
Brace initialisation disables copy constructors; write Widget b(a) to get the copy
For a non-const lvalue, T&& deduces Widget& and wins; constrain the template
std::forward cannot forward lvalues, so the template must take its argument by value
explanation: `a` is a non-const lvalue, so the forwarding reference deduces T = Widget& and produces Widget(Widget&), an exact match that beats the copy constructor's const Widget& parameter. Constrain the template, for example with `requires (!std::is_same_v<std::remove_cvref_t<T>, Widget>)` or `std::constructible_from<std::string, T>`, so it only accepts name-like arguments. The defaulted copy constructor still exists, parentheses do not change this overload resolution, and std::forward handles lvalues correctly.

title: Corruption from mismatched NDEBUG across targets
question: A header-only class has a data member guarded by `#ifndef NDEBUG` (`std::vector<int> debug_log_;`). In CMake, library `engine` is compiled with NDEBUG but `app` is not (per-target compile definitions), and objects created in engine are passed to app. Random memory corruption follows. What is the underlying problem?
options: NDEBUG must come from find_package, so defining it manually in CMake has no effect
The class has different definitions in the two targets: an ODR violation and UB
Header-only classes cannot be shared between libraries unless exported explicitly
The linker merges both definitions and keeps the larger one, which only wastes memory
explanation: The One Definition Rule requires every translation unit to see the same definition of a class used across them; a different member list means a different layout, so app's code reads and writes engine-created objects at wrong offsets, and no diagnostic is required. Keep layout-affecting macros consistent across all targets (for example through a shared interface target or the build type), or avoid configuration-dependent members in public headers. The linker does not reconcile class layouts, and header-only classes need no export.

title: std::async calls that run one after another
question: To parallelise file processing, a loop does `for (auto& f : files) std::async(std::launch::async, process, std::ref(f));`. Total time equals the sum of all calls, as if they ran sequentially. Why?
options: std::launch::async is only a hint, and the runtime chose to defer every call until the end
std::ref makes all tasks share one internal lock, so the calls serialise on that mutex
The scheduler coalesces fast-launched tasks into one thread
The discarded future's destructor blocks until its task finishes, on every iteration
explanation: A future returned by std::async with the async policy blocks in its destructor until the task completes. Because the return value is discarded, the temporary future is destroyed at the end of each full-expression, so every iteration waits for its own task. Store the futures (or use a thread pool) and wait after launching them all. With launch::async the task must run as if on a new thread, and std::ref involves no locking.

title: Crash before main after reordering CMake sources
question: `registry.cpp` defines `std::map<std::string, Factory> g_registry;`, and `plugin.cpp` defines a global `Registrar r("csv", make_csv);` whose constructor inserts into g_registry. After the sources are reordered in `add_executable`, the program crashes before main. What is the robust fix?
options: Reach the registry through a function returning a function-local static
Restore the previous source order in add_executable
Make g_registry thread_local so each thread initialises its own copy before main runs
Mark both globals inline in a header so that the linker can order their initialisation
explanation: The dynamic initialisation order of globals in different translation units is unspecified, so the Registrar may run before g_registry is constructed: the static initialisation order fiasco. A function such as `Registry& registry() { static Registry r; return r; }` constructs the registry on first use, and initialising function-local statics is thread-safe since C++11. Relying on link order is fragile, thread_local does not fix cross-TU ordering, and inline variables define no order between different variables across translation units.
